doc.title: Mike Wofford interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Then and now: the flood of jazz records
summary: LPs were scarce then, whereas now many come out hourly; they discuss why, including cheap production and home CD making.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Oh well then shortly, immediately I started grabbing everything I could. You know it’s hard to imagine a time when, if there were maybe three or four new LPs a month in the stores, that was a pretty hot month. But now you have that many in an hour coming out.
Isn’t that curious. Because the market for jazz today, as we’ve talked about that the club scene is very poor and the jazz is not the overall popular music. Yet there’s so much product.

I know I was talking with someone about that just the other day. There’s more than ever and yet the health of the music generally is not great, I mean as far as the real world of working and playing and performing and so on. I don’t know. I don’t have an answer to that. Someone said they thought it was economically a lot cheaper to produce than ever before perhaps, with modern technology, and that might have some bearing on it. I know companies used to be a lot more careful about I mean they would really screen people before they’d even consider recording them. It had to be someone who’d really paid some dues, and then they might get a chance, a shot at a record contract, at least one record. And I don’t think that’s as much the case today. I think there’s a lot more kind of readiness to record people, and take a loss if necessary, because I don’t think it’s maybe as expensive as it was to produce CD’s. Now I don’t know, you’d have to talk to someone in the business to get the numbers, but that was one theory I heard.
Well you can pretty much go out and make your own these days for not that much money too.
